issues.legal_issue: Residential accommodation used by religious members for religious instruction and related religious activity may be used principally for religious purposes even though it also serves a residential function.
material_facts: The building was a convent residence for sisters who had undergone religious training and were engaged in religious and charitable service.
The building included prayer, study, and residential spaces, and sisters in training also lived there while attending a nearby college.
The building was not rented out or used for a commercial purpose.
issues.conclusion: The convent residence qualified for the building-tax exemption because its residential use was integrally connected with religious activity.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975 exempts buildings used principally, not exclusively, for religious purposes. The relevant test is the building’s dominant use, including whether its use is directly and integrally connected with religious activity. Sections 2(e) and 2(l), read with Section 5A, support treating a building’s integrated religious use as distinct from a building used exclusively for residential purposes.

predicates.building_tax_exemption_claim: An owner seeks an exemption from building tax for a building.
predicates.religious_residents_live_there_for_relig: Members of a religious community live in the building to receive religious instruction or carry out religious activity.
predicates.building_is_commercially_leased: The building is let out for rent as a commercial use.

issues.definition: When a building-tax exemption is claimed for a building where religious residents live for religious instruction or activity, and the building is not commercially leased, the rule treats the residence as qualifying for the exemption.

issues.legal_issue: A hostel owned by an educational institution and used to accommodate its own students for study may serve an educational purpose, whether or not hostel accommodation is compulsory for institutional approval.
material_facts: The cases concerned hostels owned by educational institutions and used to accommodate their own students.
For medical and nursing institutions, regulatory requirements made hostel facilities compulsory, and students required access to hospitals for clinical training, including at night.
Other institutions also needed hostels where students came from distant areas and could not otherwise practically attend the institution.
The court distinguished institution-owned hostels for the institution’s students from buildings owned by private parties and rented to students as a commercial activity.
issues.conclusion: Institution-owned hostels accommodating the institution’s own students for their studies qualified for the exemption; privately operated commercial lodging did not qualify on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1)(b) exempts buildings used principally for educational purposes. A student hostel is within that purpose when it is owned by the educational institution, accommodates its own students, and provides accommodation connected with their pursuit of study. The connection may be necessary because of regulatory requirements or the practical needs of students attending the institution; commercial letting by a private party is different.

rule.if: building_tax_exemption_claim and hostel_owned_by_educational_institution and hostel_accommodates_its_own_students_for_study and not hostel_is_commercial_lodging_for_the_public

predicates.building_tax_exemption_claim: An owner seeks an exemption from building tax for a building.
predicates.hostel_owned_by_educational_institution: The educational institution owns the hostel building.
predicates.hostel_accommodates_its_own_students_for: The hostel accommodates students of that institution so they can pursue their studies there.
predicates.hostel_is_commercial_lodging_for_the_pub: The building is operated as commercial lodging available to students or other members of the public.

issues.definition: An institution-owned hostel used to accommodate that institution’s own students for study qualifies under the rule unless it is instead commercial lodging for the public.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficial tax exemption intended to advance religious, charitable, or educational purposes must be interpreted in a manner that gives effect to that purpose, rather than by applying the strict approach for tax exemptions generally.
material_facts: The exemption covered buildings principally used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes, as well as factories and workshops.
The court regarded the exemption for religious, charitable, and educational purposes as serving a beneficial public purpose.
The State argued that the general rule requiring strict interpretation of tax exemptions should resolve any doubt against exemption.
issues.conclusion: The exemption had to be construed purposively and liberally in light of its beneficial purpose; the general strict-interpretation rule did not displace the authorities governing beneficial exemptions.
issues.legal_principle: Union of India v. Wood Papers Ltd. (1990) 4 SCC 256 and Star Industries v. Commissioner of Customs (Imports) (2016) 2 SCC 362 describe strict construction at the stage of determining whether a subject falls within an exemption, followed by wider construction once it does. For beneficial or promotional exemptions, CST v. Industrial Coal Enterprises (1999) 2 SCC 607, State of Jharkhand v. Tata Cummins Ltd. (2006) 4 SCC 57, Pondicherry State Coop. Consumer Federation Ltd. v. Union Territory of Pondicherry (2008) 1 SCC 206, CST v. Amara Raja Batteries Ltd. (2009) 8 SCC 209, Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) v. M. Ambalal & Co. (2011) 2 SCC 74, and CCE v. Favourite Industries (2012) 7 SCC 153 support purposive, liberal construction. Commissioner of Customs v. Dilip Kumar & Co. (2018) 9 SCC 1 addressed the general rule for exemptions and did not overrule the distinct line of authority on beneficial exemptions; Quinn v. Leathem [1901] AC 495, as applied in State of Orissa v. Sudhansu Sekhar Misra (1968) 2 SCR 154, supports the proposition that a decision is authority for what it decides.

predicates.tax_exemption_claim: A person claims an exemption from tax.
predicates.exemption_serves_a_beneficial_public_pur: The exemption is intended to advance a beneficial public purpose rather than merely provide a general tax exception.
predicates.claimant_falls_within_the_purpose_of_the: The claimed use falls within the purpose the exemption is intended to advance.

issues.definition: When a tax exemption serves a beneficial public purpose and the claimed use falls within that purpose, the rule requires a purposive interpretation of the exemption.

issues.legal_issue: A court ordinarily gives deference to a High Court’s settled interpretation of a local statute, particularly when people have arranged their affairs in reliance on that interpretation.
material_facts: The appeals challenged High Court judgments interpreting a local building-tax statute.
The relevant High Court interpretations had stood for a period of time, and the court noted that people arrange their affairs based on the existing legal position.
issues.conclusion: The court considered deference to the High Court’s interpretation an additional reason to sustain the judgments under review.
issues.legal_principle: The court cited State of Gujarat v. Zinabhai Ranchhodji Darji (1972) 1 SCC 233, Bishamber Dass Kohli v. Satya Bhalla (1993) 1 SCC 566, Duroflex Coir Industries Ltd. v. CST, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 568, State of Karnataka v. G. Seenappa, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 648, and Bonam Satyavathi v. Addala Raghavulu, 1994 Supp (2) SCC 556, for the ordinary deference due to a High Court’s interpretation of a local statute, especially where that interpretation has stood the test of time.

predicates.appeal_challenges_high_court_interpretat: A party appeals against a High Court’s interpretation of a local statute.
predicates.interpretation_has_stood_over_time: The High Court’s interpretation has remained established over time.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a High Court’s interpretation of a local statute and that interpretation has remained established over time, the rule gives the interpretation deference.
